title: Business Phone System Buyer's Guide: How to Choose the Right Communication Platform
description: A practical buyer's guide to business phone systems, covering call routing, reliability, integrations, security, porting, and total cost.
author: Emily Nakamura

sections.title: Map call flows and business needs
sections.body: Document how calls arrive, route, queue, transfer, record, and escalate today. Separate needs for sales, support, reception, remote staff, and emergency or after-hours coverage. Record call volume, peak periods, regions, required numbers, and the business systems involved. A phone platform should be selected around real call flows and ownership, not only the number of features in a plan.

sections.title: Test voice quality and reliability
sections.body: Pilot with representative networks, headsets, mobile devices, and office locations. Test latency, jitter, packet loss, call transfer, hold, voicemail, and recovery when connectivity drops. Check how the service behaves during an outage and whether calls can route to an alternate device or number. Ask for clear service-status reporting and support escalation paths for business-critical calling.

sections.title: Evaluate routing and administration
sections.body: Test auto attendants, queues, ring groups, business hours, voicemail, call recording, shared lines, and number porting. Verify that non-technical administrators can change schedules and routing without breaking the main number. Define who can listen to recordings, download them, or change retention. Make sure emergency calling and location requirements are reviewed for the regions where employees work.

sections.title: Connect the tools people already use
sections.body: Check integration with CRM, help desk, calendars, contact directories, identity providers, and analytics. Test screen pops, call logging, click-to-call, and synchronization when a contact changes. Confirm how integrations handle duplicate records and failed API calls. Avoid collecting more call data than the workflow needs, and document which system is authoritative for contact information.

sections.title: Review security and compliance
sections.body: Verify SSO, MFA, role-based permissions, audit logs, encryption, call recording controls, retention, export, and data location. Review consent and notification requirements for recording with qualified legal guidance in relevant jurisdictions. Check support access and how the vendor handles incidents or account termination. A security feature listed on a general product page may be restricted to a particular plan.

sections.title: Model the full cost
sections.body: Include licenses, phone numbers, domestic and international calling, toll-free usage, recording storage, contact center features, integrations, hardware, porting, and support. Verify current plan limits and rates directly with the vendor. Model peak usage and the cost of adding new locations or temporary staff. Include administration and migration time, not just the advertised per-user price.

sections.title: Plan number porting and cutover
sections.body: Create a porting inventory, confirm account ownership and required documents, and schedule the cutover with a fallback plan. Test incoming and outgoing calls, emergency routing, voicemail, caller ID, queues, and after-hours rules before switching the main number. Keep the old service available until the new routing is accepted. Assign a single cutover owner and a way to report failures quickly.

sections.title: Selection checklist
sections.body: Choose a provider only after the pilot demonstrates reliable call quality, correct routing, workable administration, required integrations, and acceptable total cost. Document emergency procedures, number ownership, support contacts, and exit options. Reassess when the organization adds regions, call-center workflows, or new recording requirements.
